subtopic: GREAT LAKES-STATEMENT ON CANADA-UNITED STATES MINISTERIAL MEETING IN WASHINGTON

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of Fisheries and Forestry):
subtopic: GREAT LAKES-STATEMENT ON CANADA-UNITED STATES MINISTERIAL MEETING IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to report to the House on the outcome of a Canada-United States ministerial meeting on Great Lakes pollution which was held in Washington yesterday, and which was attended by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) and myself, along with Mr. Kerr, Ontario Minister of Energy and Resources Management, and by Dr. Victor Goldbloom, minister responsible for environmental quality in the Quebec government. The United States government was represented by a cabinet level delegation headed by Mr. Russell Train, who is the chairman of the council on environmental quality, and Mr. William Ruckelshaus, the head of the environmental protection agency; the United States delegation also included senior representatives of the Great Lakes states governments.
At our meeting yesterday we agreed that Canada and the United States should conclude a formal agreement which would have the objective of cleaning up the Great Lakes and protecting them in the future. We also reached general agreement on the contents of this agreement, on the basis of recommendations by a joint working group which was established by a first ministerial meeting on Great Lakes problems held in Ottawa last June. We
agreed that negotiations should begin right away on the precise text of this agreement, in the expectation that it can be ready for signature in the early autumn.
The decisions we reached yesterday reflect the determination of the governments concerned, at the federal, province and state levels, to take action to deal with the critical pollution situation in many areas of the Great Lakes, especially in Lake Erie and its connecting waterways. The proposed agreement will be solidly based on extensive scientific investigations by the International Joint Commission, and on recommendations submitted by the commission in a report which was tabled in the House in January.
This agreement will establish common water quality objectives which will be based on objectives proposed by the International Joint Commission. On the basis of these common objectives, the governments concerned will establish compatible and legally enforceable standards; and they will also commit themselves to carry out the pollution control programs and other measures to achieve the common objectives within agreed time periods. These programs will include accelerated municipal and industrial pollution control programs; the reduction of phosphorus inputs, which is causing particularly serious problems in Lake Erie; the elimination of mercury and other toxic heavy metals from discharges; control of thermal pollution and pollution from radioactive wastes; control of pollution from pesticides and the development of controls for pollution from combined sewer overflows.
This agreement will also provide for effective and compatible regulations throughout the whole Great Lakes system designed to reduce the risk of pollution from shipping and land transportation, including regulations to control waste discharges by ships. The International Joint Commission will be requested to conduct an intensive investigation into pollution from agriculture, forestry and other land source pollution and to create new arrangements for the better co-ordination of water quality research.
The International Joint Commission will be given additional responsibility and authority in the surveillance of the water quality in the Great Lakes and the control of programs of all the governments concerned. The commission will be requested to make recommendations to the governments on the improvement of their pollution control legislation and programs. We agreed to provide the International Joint Commission with the additional staff and other resources it will need to carry out its expanded role.
At our meeting yesterday we also announced a number of co-operative measures which will be put into effect immediately. These include a new joint contingency plan which could be implemented quickly in the event of a

June 11, 1971
Great Lakes Pollution
major spill of oil or other hazardous substances. Under this new joint plan the national plans of each country and the Ontario contingency plan will be co-ordinated, so that there will be a joint response to any emergency situation under procedures and arrangements agreed in advance. It was also agreed yesterday that the International Joint Commission should be requested to make a thorough study of pollution problems in Lake Huron and Lake Superior, similar to their recently completed study of the lower lakes pollution problems.
This proposed agreement on Great Lakes water quality should lead to an early improvement in the condition of Great Lakes water, especially in the lower lakes area. The United States will be assuming firm commitments to carry out by 1975 accelerated municipal and industrial control programs, and these programs should greatly reduce the extensive transboundary pollution which exists in many areas. These programs will require expenditures for pollution abatement by the United States many times larger than on the Canadian side.
It will, however, be necessary to accelerate municipal and industrial programs on the Canadian side, particularly in the lower lakes area, so that by 1975 our programs in Ontario will be adequate to achieve the agreed common water quality objectives. I have discussed this matter with Mr. Kerr, because the implementation of many of the Canadian commitments under the proposed Canada-United States agreement will be the joint responsibility of the federal government and the government of Ontario. We have agreed that the apportionment of responsibility among the Canadian government, the government of Ontario and the municipalities concerned for financing the required accelerated program of improvements to municipal sewage treatment facilities in the lower lakes area will be the subject of a detailed agreement to be negotiated between the Canadian government and the government of Ontario. These negotiations will commence right away, since we shall need to conclude our agreement with Ontario before entering into the proposed agreement with the United States next autumn.
It was the view of all who participated at our meeting yesterday that the proposed agreement and the other measures we announced represent a comprehensive and positive response to the recommendations of the International Joint Commission. It will be a precedent for the two countries in dealing with other environmental problems along our boundary, and it will also be a model for other countries in attempting to control pollution across international borders.
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I should like to table the joint communique which was issued at the conclusion of our meeting in Washington yesterday.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-STATEMENT ON CANADA-UNITED STATES MINISTERIAL MEETING IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by welcoming the minister back from his Washington tour. It is a long time since we have seen the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), however. I should like to commend the minister for the promptness with which he reported on this
matter to Parliament. I think this is the way ministers should relate themselves to this chamber.
I also say that we join in approval of the declaration of intent which followed this meeting and we look forward to the more concrete and precise statements which the minister has outlined in this program.
I note with some little concern that there was some imbalance in the joint talks. The minister uses the expression "cabinet level delegation". I had thought the minister would be meeting with ministers of the United States government, but that was not the case.
I note no projection concerning the cost of this program, and this matter will concern us, but I do commend the steps that have been taken by this government, the government of Ontario and the United States. I do hope-that the minister's forecast that something will be done soon will be borne out. This will be an extremely difficult job; much has to be done. I think it was very wise to-give the International Joint Commission greater authority, greater scope of action and, of course, additional trained and qualified personnel in this new and very important role which they must carry through.
I am sorry, however, that this meeting which was-designed to be a high level discussion on the TAPS route apparently took no cognizance of that very important matter. We were told on May 17 and on May 26, despite the Prime Minister's lapse of memory yesterday, that there would be a ministerial discussion on June 10 on the TAPS route. I find not a single reference to TAPS in the minister's statement nor in the communique. I wonder whether, instead of accusing the member for Hillsborough of having a lapse of memory the government itself is losing interest in this very important matter. The government has failed to fulfil a firm commitment given, in the House to discuss the TAPS route. We are allowed to gather from the press inferentially that tacked on at the end of the formal discussions the matter was mentioned in an informal way. This is not sufficient for a problem of such great concern as the trans-Alaska pipeline route with all its potential hazards to the people and the coast of British Columbia.
On this matter I take exception, express concern, voice alarm and say to the minister charged with this matter, who is from British Columbia, that it should have been taken up and that the government of British Columbia should have been represented at that part of the meeting just as the governments of other provinces were represented on those matters dealing with the Great Lakes. The government is remiss in this regard. I think it must take seriously the question of the TAPS route, get its ministers together soon, outline its policy, make a statement in the House and then go vigorously to Washington and present the point of view of the Canadian government and the Canadian people on the terrible dangers of the proposed TAPS route. For this omission I criticize the minister most severely.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-STATEMENT ON CANADA-UNITED STATES MINISTERIAL MEETING IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of our group welcome the report the minister has given the House on the conference held yesterday

June 11, 1971

with representatives of the United States in connection with the problem of pollution on the Great Lakes. It is very encouraging that the talks have progressed at least to the point where it is expected that a formal *agreement will be signed this fall in respect of measures to be taken to clean up the pollution in this great waterway.
There are one or two points on which I should like to have clar.fication from the minister some time within the next few days. 1 note in the press release that the committee yesterday agreed to accept most of the recommendations of the International Joint Commission which were made last December, its report having been presented to us last January. I should like the minister to tell us some t.me before the end of June which of these recommendations were not acceptable to the committee because somet mes such recommendations are extremely important. I think Canadians are entitled to know which of the recommendations did not meet with general acceptance by the two groups which met yesterday.
As I looked over the report of the International Joint Commission very quickly to refresh my memory, I noted that the commission pointed out very clearly that one of the keys to keeping the Great Lakes free of pollution was control over the rivers and the streams running into the Great Likes from the states and the provinces bordering the lakes. They pointed out that controls must be exercised over the rivers and streams running into these great bodies of water. In this regard provincial jurisdiction and the jurisdiction of the various states that border the Great Lakes are involved. If anything crystal clear [DOT]came out of the meeting held yesterday and the recommendations which the minister read to the House today, it is that we must have national standards for Canada and strong international standards which must be enforced nationally. The states bordering the Great Lakes cannot be allowed to carry on their own enforcement. The whole area is involved in the pollution problem and one body must exercise some kind of authority in regard to enforcement throughout the whole area. I point out that there is a lesson here for members of the House that we have to progress nationally and make sure that standards are set up which can be enforced in such a manner as to cure the pollution problems in the Great Lakes.
I should like to make one comment on the remarks made by the speaker for the official opposition on the TAPS program and the proposed tanker route down the west coast of Canada. I feel that some reference should have been made to this vital and important problem. It is one which the government must tackle without delay. I hope the government will take a firm stand and present its views to the United States government before an agreement is reached which will allow the TAPS line to be built across Alaska and the establishment of a tanker route down the west coast of North America. We hope we will have some information on this matter before the end of June.
That is all I have to say. Again I should like to commend the minister and the group who went to Washing-

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-STATEMENT ON CANADA-UNITED STATES MINISTERIAL MEETING IN WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we appreciate this statement from the Minister of Fisheries to the effect that an agreement has been signed between the United States and Canada. In my view, this agreement is a striking example of co-operation between neighbouring nations on a very current problem, pollution. We are not talking about pollution of streams but rather about pollution of major inland waters, like the Greak Lakes and, hence, probably the great St. Lawrence River which flows through the whole of the province of Quebec.
It was a pleasure to hear the minister say that the Quebec government had delegated Dr. Victor Goldbloom as its representative at the meetings. I regret however that Ontario was not represented at that conference, for Ontario actually borders extensively on the Great Lakes.
At any rate, Mr. Speaker, this agreement, I am sure, will help in cleaning up our Canadian waters and will tend to protect our waterways from the pollution which we are currently faced with.
Therefore, we welcome this announcement and we urge the minister and the government to pursue their activities along these lines so that Canadian waters may be cleaned up.

KINGSTON-DISTURBANCE IN WOMEN'S PRISON-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I ask the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The immediacy of the motion is sparked by the disturbance, yesterday and Wednesday, in the Kingston Penitentiary for Women. Of that disturbance this House knows only what members have read in the papers and heard on the air, but it is only the latest in a series of riots that have erupted with frightening regularity in our prisons. They have brought with them death and destruction. I think that surely in a civilized society, ruled by the standards of religion and morality, all people should be treated with justice and fairness. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell):
That the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs be authorized to visit our prison institutions, in particular the Kingston Penitentiary for Women, Kingston Penitentiary and Millhaven, to question prisoners and members of the staffs, and to make such other inquiries as to the committee seem necessary.

speechtext:
I can assure the House it is not a Freudian slip, Mr. Speaker, it is just an order from the boss. I am getting further and further from the left, and I can see I am going to be influenced all afternoon by the very positive force opposite.
During the committee hearings the United Auto Workers pointed out what they thought was an anomaly in the act. This was after we had discussed the exercise of the 15 weeks' benefits over a period of 29 weeks. There was also some discussion of the period being terminated after four weeks without claim. It was presumed, of course, that the individual would have been working or some thing of this nature.
As a result of that discussion in committee, it occurred to the department and to my staff that we were unintentionally penalizing certain workers or creating a situation where certain people in the work force could be penalized. As you are aware, the major attachment claim entitlement is three weeks' payment, then 12 weeks and then 10 weeks for a total of 25 weeks' benefits. The first 15 weeks can be drawn over a period of 29 weeks. After that period, the 10 weeks' entitlement must be drawn consecutively, and I think we all agree with this. However, this section provides for four weeks in this period for which no benefits are paid, and then the individual must re-establish a claim. That is, he must prove a minimum of eight weeks' attachment. This is what the United Auto Workers complained about and suggested could, in fact, be a disincentive to work. The effect of the amendment that I am proposing, with the unanimous consent of the House, of course, would be to withdraw this restriction; that is, first where the individual was fully employed during that period or where no payment was due to previous overpayments. What we are saying in effect is that if you are not drawing unemployment insurance for four weeks as a result of working, you are not penalized by having to re-establish your claim, thus losing your two weeks' benefits.
An hon. member for the opposition pointed this out to me a week or so ago, and I think he was quite right. Consequently, this would be a disadvantage. So a worker who had an opportunity while unemployed and drawing
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 insurance benefits to pick up four weeks' work would have the tendency to reject the work, because if he accepted it this would mean that when the four weeks were up and he went back to the unemployment insurance office he would have to lose two weeks' benefits all over again and go through the same procedure. Rather than do this he would pass up the opportunity to work for four weeks.
We say if you are divorced from unemployment insurance benefits for four weeks, specifically because you are working during that time, you will not be penalized and you can return precisely as though you had not accepted the part-time job. This is the sole purpose of the amendment and I hope the House concurs.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I think the hon. gentleman who just spoke is quite accurate in his analysis of the existing clause and the purpose behind the clause. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) mentioned, this matter was debated at great length in the committee. Perhaps I might have a minute to explain the philosophy behind the whole thing. Periodically, we should be reminded that unemployment insurance is not something which exists exclusively for the benefit of the workers. The fund is financed by the employers and the employees of the country. The general rule is that we have no intention to use our unemployment insurance fund to finance a strike. Therefore, one of the basic things the commission makes certain of is that we do not finance strikes out of funds that are equally proportioned between employer and employee. In other words, I do not think anyone would want to finance a strike with moneys which partly
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) .1
belong to the employers of the country. I believe that is clear-cut.
However, we go a little further in protecting the fund. We might take the example of a person who is not a member of a union but who became unemployed as a result of a strike over which he had no control. He may be a janitor or a person sweeping the floors. He may come to the commission and say he is out of work because of a strike in which he is not involved. Our answer to him would be that, even though he is not a member of the union and may not have a direct voice in the decision to go on strike, he would benefit from the end result of the dispute because the collective agreement covers not only the unionized employees but all employees. While he may not have a direct participation in the strike he does have, in most cases, a financial interest in the outcome because the end result would mean an increase in his income. If that same company owned three, four or five different operations or, let us say, had activities spread over various branches, and if these branches were affected by a strike or were in some way affected by lack of material and things of this nature, then in that case the employees of these other branches would not be deprived of their unemployment insurance.
We have a case in Flin Flon, for instance, where the craft unions are on strike and the steel workers are not. The steel workers will not benefit by the settlement of the craft workers' dispute and therefore, at the moment, are eligible for unemployment insurance because the plant has been closed down as the result of an action over which they had no control and because when the financial settlement is reached they will in no way be involved. So, they are eligible. Really, we are protecting the fund, but we give as much latitude as possible to the commission to make certain that no one is intentionally deprived of his normal right. Fortunately, because of the way the commission operates, there is sufficient jurisprudence which has been accumulated over the past 20 or 30 years which can be used by the officials, referees and umpires in making certain that justice is done in the case of people who may not be members of a union but who are affected by the labour dispute.
So, I must recommend that this amendment be rejected because, although I understand and sympathize with the reasoning of the hon. member who proposed the amendment, and who unfortunately cannot be here today, I must remind myself and others must remind themselves that we have an immediate obligation to the employers as well as the employees of this country who participate financially to the same extent to make sure we do not finance a strike with the employers' money. On the other hand, we cannot encourage people who remain outside a union and refuse to participate in any shape or form to come lamely to the unemployment insurance commission and say that if they had given in there would not have been a strike so, therefore, they would like to have the unemployment insurance money. We cannot encourage this because eventually these people will get the pay raise or the advantage of the improved conditions which the collective agreement will bring about.

Mr. Speaker, if I did not quite grasp the hon. member's point, I am sure he will understand. I do not know offhand of any cases where a union would be legally on strike when that strike would not be binding on all members of the union. I think this rarely occurs. I mentioned the strike at Flin Flon in which the steel workers who have completed their collective agreement and who are prepared to work are out of work because the plant is now struck as a result of a labour dispute between the employer and members of a group of unions called craft unions. The craft union members are not entitled to unemployment insurance because the strike is the result of their direct decision, but the steel workers are entitled to unemployment insurance because they had no participation in the decision-making that brought about the strike, nor will they benefit in any way from the ultimate result of the strike in so far as increased pay or benefits are concerned. The criteria are, first, whether the person involved has a voice in respect of the creation of the strike and, second, even if he is not a member of the union and did not have a voice whether he will eventually benefit from the strike.
In passing, I might point out that through jurisprudence and through our past decisions, a precedent has been established that when people are laid off as a result of a deliberate slow-down prior to a strike, thus reducing productivity or impeding the productivity of that particular employer with the result that he may have to cut back his work force, if these people apply for unemployment insurance and if it can be proven that this has been due to a deliberate slow-down, they cannot draw unemployment insurance. Sometimes these cases go to appeal. Sometimes a decision is made on the side of the employee and sometimes on the side of the employer. There is an effort to maintain a balance between the employer and the employee. The two basic rules are, first, that one should not benefit in any way materially from the end result of the labour dispute and, second, that one should have had no voice in fomenting a strike

speechtext:
I have been interested for a long time in the interpretation by the Unemployment Insurance Commission of the words "directly interested in". This has, in many cases, been used in various ways and changes have taken place for various reasons in the decisions that the commission has made. In the matter of financing, I presume the minister is not referring to persons who are making a donation. He is more interested in the direct financing of a situation and this probably has a different connotation. Many unions assist
in the financing of a labour dispute and yet they are in no way involved in the process of making the decision that there will be a strike, or whatever the negotiations may be, nor in any way would they receive remuneration from that. The minister has made decisions in these situations, such as the one he made with regard to the Hudson Bay Mining to separate the trades and the industrial union involved. These decisions have not always been made by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. On many occasions their decision was different.
This is one of the reasons that my colleagues and I are concerned about leaving in the words "directly interested in". If you work for the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Corporation, obviously you will be directly interested in what they do and what are the financial and other implications of their actions. Whatever the company does will have some effect on what happens to you if you are one of their employees, even if you are in a different area or a different town. This has been misinterpreted many times, and it lends itself to various interpretations. I have no qualms about the minister making the right decision, but I have many qualms about the commission making a decision. They have made various decisions on both sides. Sometimes they have allowed payment of benefits, and sometimes they have not when, in my opinion, the reasons were unclear. For this reason many thousands of regulations will have to be made under the bill. These regulations will be in the form of decisions made at various stages. Each may become a precedent. I am sure the minister is aware of cases, apparently identical cases, where totally different conclusions were reached. The words here are subject to varying interpretations, and I do not think they will achieve what the minister wants.
I am also interested in some protection being provided against a situation in which a number of employees might decide they were going to have a holiday and collect unemployment insurance while on holiday. I am sure this might be arranged by a small number of employees acting together in one very large plant. If we leave the words "directly interested in" in the bill, I know that the umpires and all others involved in the decision making process in the Unemployment Insurance Commission may interpret them in different ways. The minister mentioned the Hudson Bay decision in which he had some interest, but I know of at least half a dozen cases where that decision was reversed. Once this bill is enacted we, as Members of Parliament, will have no influence on the decisions that are made. We will be left totally at the mercy of the interpretations that are made.
I know of one case where one union did have two bargaining units operating in a plant. As an industrial worker I was always of the opinion that there were three levels in a plant, the management, the office staff, and the other workers. I had no relationship with the office staff or management, but management did have close relations with office staff. At the Hollinger Mines we organized the office staff into a separate unit of the United Steel Work-
(Mr. Barnett.]

ers, but when the other section went on strike the office staff was not able to draw unemployment insurance. The office staff had not attended the strike meetings and had no influence on the strike decision. We were using the CWS program and a wage structure that did not apply to them. They may have been interested in seeing that members of an associated local of the Steel Workers did not get beaten, but they had no financial interest in the strike. Yet the commission interpretation went against them.
The minister and other hon. members who have had anything to do with labour negotiations are well aware of the problem. If we do not amend the bill, then the Commission will introduce regulations that will change our interpretation of it. I speak from experience of attending tribunals and finding the regulations totally changed from what I had expected them to be. If we leave the words "directly interested" in the bill, the Commission may make whatever interpretations it deems warranted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the minister would agree with me that basically what we are concerned about when discussing a bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Plan is that the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the operations of the plan should be as neutral as possible in any situation involving a labour dispute. All we are concerned about is how to achieve this.
Certainly, in the union to which I belong there is a feeling that since the inception of the Unemployment Insurance Commission the jurisprudence that has developed, as a result of Commission interpretations and umpires' decisions, is weighted on the side of the employer interests and against the worker interests. Because of that widespread feeling, I think this is a matter that should receive the closest scrutiny. I am sure it did receive a great deal of discussion in the committee, but apparently my colleague from Moose Jaw was not satisfied that the wording of the bill will create the neutrality desired.
As I read the proposed amendment, I think it is pretty clear that the hon. member wants a distinct statement stipulating that in future umpire decisions should be even-Steven down the line. The way the bill and the existing act are worded means that the onus of proof is on the worker-and this would apply even under the terms of the proposed amendment-to establish that he is not directly involved or participating in the labour dispute that has caused the stoppage of work.
I would remind the minister of some of the situations that developed as a result of the towboat dispute on the coast of British Columbia. I am convinced that the employees in some of the logging operations in the northwest part of Vancouver Island were not directly involved and were not supporting that dispute. But they were laid off because the towboats were tied up. Their claims for unemployment insurance have been in process, and the last word I heard was that there is soon to be an umpire's hearing. Those workers have been left up in the
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 air for months, wondering whether they are going to get the benefits they feel they are entitled to as a result of being laid off by the companies because work operations could not continue due to the tie up of the towboats.
When we talk about this question of financing and participating directly or indirectly as the clause is worded in the bill, this leads to almost any kind of interpretation in the future by an umpire. The whole concept of the labour movement is that it is interrelated. I have voted many times to send a contribution to workers on strike somewhere else. If one wants to take these words literally the fact that a local union has voted $1,000 or $25 to support a group of striking workers in another place, could lead to an umpire's decision that any member of that union who happened to be laid off could be denied benefits because he was financing and had a direct interest in that other labour dispute, though it might be on the other side of the continent.
I do not think the existing jurisprudence has gone in that direction, but this is so complex a problem that only a full-time professional could keep a clear picture in mind of where the matter stands or where it is heading. I cannot understand why the minister is insisting that this phrase be retained. The amendment would provide that a worker would have to prove that he was not directly involved or participating in the labour dispute that caused the stoppage. That seems to put it fairly clearly from the point of view of any future decisions by an umpire on what at times are going to be pretty difficult lines of demarcation.
We all know that under certain circumstances groups of workers who have not been involved in a labour dispute have to make a decision about whether they will handle hot goods or hot cargo. The interpretation of whether or not that action would involve them in the dispute is one on which there may be some disagreement. If the words about financing and direct interest are left in the clause it seems to me that the possibility of a worker proving that he is not involved is weighted against the worker. I urge the minister to recognize that there is no provision that the employer has to prove the worker is involved; the onus is on the worker to prove that he is not involved before he can accept benefit. In a sense, that weights the application of the act in the direction of protecting the employer interests against having their contributions to the fund used to assist workers with whom they may have a dispute. That is one of the considerations the minister should have in assessing the merits of a clause such as this, that you start by putting the onus of proof on the worker. It should be made as simple and as straightforward as possible for the worker to prove it. The wording in the act on which an umpire is going to have to base decisions should enable him to draw a line that is as clear and simple as it can be.
We hope that, as a result of the new act, some of the very messy and unhappy situations that have developed

The hon. member for Hamilton Wes* (Mr. Alexander) also moves Motion No. 13 as follows:
That Bill C-229, unemployment insurance in Canada, be amended by deleting clause 65 at pages 42 and 43.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I believe that during the committee hearings members found that, as a result of this new experience which has been brought into the Unemployment Insurance Act, the vast majority of the members questioned the usefulness and the acceptability of what is called the experience rating or the merit rating system which is being introduced by the government.
I recall that yesterday the minister accused members of this party as well as hon. members of the New Democratic Party of being confused inasmuch as we were continually reaching conflicting conclusions. It seems to me the minister has now indicated to the House, and I accept this philosophy in that regard, that many of us must be our brothers' keepers. On the other hand we said we should abide by the universality of the unemployment insurance scheme. It seems to me that rather than being confused on this side of the House it was the government which is confused because the government has now indicated that it is not interested in universality when it comes down to industry. They believe we should get away from the pooling of risks by saying there should be a penalty placed upon industry as a result of high lay-offs.
What concerns many of these people in industry who are making a great contribution to the ultimate destiny of this country is that in many instances lay-offs are beyond the r control. For example, I do not want to become political this afternoon but one of the reasons industries occasionally lay off people is the fiscal and monetary policy of the government; there can be no question of that. This is something beyond the control of employers. The external ramifications of capital and money exchanges certainly affect lay-off patterns, as do seasonal adjustments.
If we increase premium rates of employers, the extra cost must of necessity be passed on to the consumer. For the life of me, I cannot understand the thinking of this government when it says that we should pool the risk. After all, they brought in an additional one million people to enable them to pool the risk. They have included in the plan school teachers, firemen, nurses, public servants and armed forces personnel so that the risk can be pooled. The government feels that some industries, perhaps through their inability to compete, should be penalized or driven out of business, but at the same time it forgets that the main theme running behind the entire act is that there should be a pooling of risk and that universality should prevail.
This is one occasion when we found that even labour took a pretty dim view of what the government was doing in this instance. I admit that the senior chamber of commerce took the opposite view and said there should.

Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 be a pooling of risk. But what is important is that the vast majority of the briefs submitted on this matter were very much opposed to the introduction of experience rating.
It is also of extreme importance that the Gill report dealt with this question. I do not know whether the Gill report is relevant or not, but I do know that he took a pretty dim view of experience rating. I should like to refer to some of the arguments Mr. Gill put forward for the benefit of the government dealing with this particular clause. The Gill report stated:
It will, we think, suffice for present purposes to indicate, as follows, the main reasons why we do not recommend the adoption of a system of merit rating.
We favour a system of broad pooling of risk and this is the foundation of our recommendations for universal coverage. We believe that the frictional unemployment that can properly be taken care of by a plan of unemployment insurance is a more or less normal phenomenon of a free economic system, but it emerges strongly in certain industries and occupations in the system and scarcely at all in others. This variation is not, however, the result of particular management decisions. It is, instead, a function beyond the control of the employers concerned.
The statement "beyond the control of the employers concerned" is very important in this context. Further the report states that merit rating-
__would have the result of raising the contribution rates for
some of the basic industries that play an important part in Canadian export trade: this would put them at a competitive disadvantage in the international markets.
A further point made by the report is this:
We have not observed any decisive evidence to substantiate the claim that the operation of a merit rating system would have any significant effect in reducing unemployment.
I am putting forward these points so that the people of this country, as well as my colleagues in the House, understand what is taking place. Another point made by Mr. Gill is this:
There is some evidence to suggest that the existence of merit rating encourages undesirable practices on the part of some employers. They may tend to oppose claims merely for the sake of improving their position with respect to merit rating. They may oppose socially desirable extensions of the unemployment insurance scheme for the same reasons, and they may indulge in practices relating to hiring and firing of employees designed to minimize the effect on the unemployment insurance plan.
As I said earlier, the Canadian Labour Congress is very interested in the last point. They indicated that they would oppose merit rating because of this danger. Other criticisms can be made of merit rating, and I would refer to one in particular. Merit rating has a regional and structural bias. Government officials insist that, industry by industry, merit rating is administratively and politically Impossible. However, juxtapositioning all firms against an average national lay-off rate would heavily favour mature central Canadian business and industrial structures and would actively harm growth and depressed areas. Growth industries have higher lay-off rates simply because of their dynamism. Many stagnant industries have low lay-off rates and would be rewarded even

though they often require, according to government policy, swift, efficient mobility.
Another criticism that can be made is that merit rating may bias hiring practices. The incentive, if it worked, could bring direct hardship to the very people it aims to assist-working people in search of quasi-permanent or permanent employment.
Other objections have been made to experience rating, which is why we on this side of the House deem it advisable to put before the House criticisms that have been directly voiced very vehemently and strenuously by those concerned. It is not going to help the employer, it is not going to help the employee, and the ultimate payer, as usual, will be the taxpayer who has to absorb the additional cost of any increase in premium as a result of experience rating being applied in any particular industry.
I am sure the minister and his colleagues will tell me that I have not made a bad speech but that once again I am off the beam; that things have to be this way because some industries are taking advantage of a good thing. But let me repeat that pooling a risk and universality are at the basis of the unemployment insurance plan. Starting with that premise-and I do not think anyone can disagree with the premise-you cannot then turn around and say that you must make an exception in this particular instance. With all respect, this then brings into question your credibility. I am not being offensive in saying that, but this argument does have us on this side puzzled. Without pursuing the matter further and becoming too repetitious, may I conclude by saying motions Nos. 12 and 13 are being moved primarily to eliminate what I call this very offensive clause in terms of its effects on the Canadian economy.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support what was said by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and to congratulate him on going further afield than his own particular locality. He is taking an interest in other parts of the country that are not as well developed as his home city and province. There are, of course, vast areas of the province of Ontario that would be adversely affected by this legislation, as well as the area of the country that I have the honour to represent.
I should like to say it escapes me how the bill, as proposed, will encourage stable employment in types of industries mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton West because in most cases these industries are totally dependent on factors outside their control. Of course, the major factor in that regard is the weather. The weather pretty well dictates the operations of the construction industry. We are making progress toward extending the construction season into a year-round business but, the fact remains, winter construction in the climate which prevails in most areas in this country is more expensive than in spring, summer and fall.
June 11, 1971

Apart from the construction industry, we have a problem in respect of another major industry in the country being affected by the weather, namely, the agricultural industry. It is completely dependent upon the seasons. Farm labourers are subject to the provisions of this bill. I do not think it can be argued that they will not find themselves in an industry which will have a bad merit rating regarding lay-offs. Once the harvesting of any particular crop is completed, a great number of farm labourers are laid off. This can only result in higher costs to the employer, being the farmer. He is already subject to a terrible cost-price scheme. It has been admitted by both sides of the House that the farmer is in no position to pass on this cost. In some seasonal industries, such as construction. I suppose it can be argued that this cost can be passed on. This might get the business itself off the hook, but it does not get the consumer, or the people we represent, off the hook. We should have some consideration for them.
One of my basic objections to this bill is that generally speaking it will increase costs throughout. In this bill, we find an added means of increasing the cost in what I would consider to be a totally, unacceptable and unjustifiable way. In addition to weather conditions, I think my hon. friend mentioned pressures or conditions creating instability of employment in certain areas. We have found that, for the past year or so, it has been a firm policy of the government to discourage construction in certain areas of this country. The city of Calgary, part of which I represent, is in the position of being discriminated against in respect of depreciation as a result of a desire to cool off the economy. I might say in passing, it has had a very good effect, but the construction industry in that city has suffered as a result of this conscious policy of the government.
I do not see how the imposition of higher employee contributions will help to stabilize employment in the construction industry in places like Calgary, when it is singled out from other cities in the country for discrimination by the government with a view to creating unemployment.
I agree also with the hon. member for Hamilton West that this legislation seems to be based on the view that industry is developing to the same extent throughout the country and we have a homogeneous working force. I suppose the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) would be very happy with this aspect of the legislation because his view would seem to indicate that all industry should be concentrated in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and that the outlying areas of the country should be forgotten. I am sorry I cannot take that position. I urge the government to have some consideration for the growth areas of this country, and accept this amendment which would remove a real discrimination, particularly against the construction and agricultural sectors of the economy.

Mr. Speaker, in so far as these two amendments before us are designed to eliminate experience rating from the new Unemployment Insurance Act, we shall support them. We
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 debated this matter at great length in committee and I do not think it is necessary to rehash that debate at the report stage. In an effort to achieve that goal, may I say simply that there are three main reasons for my opposition to experience rating.
In the first place, employment conditions are to a very large extent beyond the control of the employers. Some spokesmen for experience rating have tried to relate this situation to workmen's compensation where there is a form of experience rating. I suggest that employers can control the safety conditions under which their employees work and can control the number of accidents that take place. So far as the economy of the country is concerned, on which employment is based, that is to a large extent beyond the control of employers. There are various regional and seasonal factors that come into the picture, but we think that because this sort of thing is beyond the control of employers it is unfair to impose experience rating.
The second reason for our opposition to this measure is the fact that the Canadian Labour Congress and other representatives of labour have expressed the view that this would lead to an abuse. An employer who might need a certain number of employees would refrain from hiring them temporarily lest the firing of them shortly thereafter would spoil his record. We think abuses of that kind are possible and we should not encourage them by this so-called experience rating. We think there are hiring practices in reverse which are an abuse, but that they can be dealt with by an amendment such as the minister has made to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, which we hope will be copied in provincial statutes.
My third reason for opposing this is that if we are going to permit employers to pay lower premiums because of a better record than others, we will have the argument from employees that those who have had long periods without drawing unemployment insurance benefits will feel their premiums should be reduced. This is a one-sided proposition and we feel this is a defect. As I have sa d, we went into this at great length and argued it with most of the delegates who appeared before us. We tried to persuade the government to drop the whole idea of experience rating. Since we did not succeed there we are indicating that is still our position, and we shall do so again by voting for these two amendments.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate in this debate for just a few minutes. I begin by commending the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) for the amendments he has proposed. As a member from the Atlantic region of Canada, I feel that the legislation as proposed by the minister will only place one more impediment in the way of industry in that part of Canada. I feel as a result of this legislation these industries will continue to have more than their share of difficulties, day in and day out, in maintaining themselves in business.

June 11. 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
I think this places an extra burden on the shoulders of the employer concerning what he should or should not do in given circumstances. I would be fearful that what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) alluded to might happen. An employer who had been trying to make up his mind concerning whether or not he should take on additional staff for a short period of time would look at the merit system and say to himself that if he did this he might become involved in difficulty. He might consider that it might involve an extra expense, whereas if he used his present staff or kept his staff to a minimum and did not provide additional employment even for a short period of time, he would not be involved in this extra expense. Therefore, this system might work against a great many people in our part of Canada who wish to secure work even for a short period of time. In many instances many people in our labour force are under-employed. These people will now discover they will have less opportunity to secure employment, even for short periods of time. I do not want to see this happen.
I believe there is something else involved here which is even more basic. I refer to the fact that we are living in a capitalist system in this country in which we say to the employer and the unions, in effect, that they must work out a system whereby between them they will know best how industries can operate and how they can secure the best return on their investment. However, we also say we will interfere. We tell them that unless they operate in such a way as to provide constant and stable employment for their employees, whether there is work for them or not and whether or not it brings them return, we will impose upon them a special tax which they will have to pay. I know in my constituency, which is in the agricultural area, we are involved to a very substantial degree in the production of small berries such as blueberries, strawberries and so on. There are frozen food plants which operate there and provide not-year around employment but employment for a specific period of time. People have come to expect this. Certain people involve themselves in this type of employment. They arrange their schedule so that they can work here and do other things at other times.
Now, the people who operate the frozen food plants and other operations of this type will find themselves forced to bear additional costs in carrying out their operations. In facing these additional costs, there is only one conclusion for them to reach. They will have to tell the consumer they are facing additional cost because of the new unemployment insurance legislation and that, therefore, the consumer will have to pay a higher price for the same product than was the case in the past. The cost of living will go up and up and up, as it has been doing all along. In many ways, the cost of living in this country is going up because of the unwarranted interference by government into the private sector of the economy. This is a glaring example of what is happening and will continue to happen so long as the government insists on this type of legislation. So far as I am concerned, the hon.
member for Hamilton West has been very persuasive in his arguments concerning why this clause should not be accepted in its present form. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has indicated that so far as he knows labour does not want this merit system.
Why does the government insist upon adding additional burdens on the backs of industries which are having so much difficulty today in surviving? If I might anticipate, if this budget comes in and places many new taxes on the back of industry, just where is industry going? What will happen and how will we ever produce a boyant economy that will look after the hundreds of thousands of people who are in the labour force today and who are looking for work. How can we do this if we continuously heap on the shoulders of industry additional burdens and taxes industry could get along without? In view of the fact that labour itself is neither looking for nor asking for this, and indeed is objecting to the system, why should we be adamant in imposing it upon them or upon the industries which must survive if we are to produce employment in this country to look after the labour force. I cannot quite understand why the minister is so adamant about the merit system. I really do not believe it will be beneficial to either industry or labour. I believe the minister should give very serious consideration to supporting the amendment which has been proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton West.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not elaborate further on the reasons advanced by my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) in proposing the motion other than to say I agree with everything he said about the bad features of including a system of merit rating in this legislation. I heartily agree with him that it does nothing for the plan. It is a bad principle. It is not consistent with the rest of the bill. There is no merit rating, for example, so far as the employees are concerned. The employee pays the same rate regardless of how many times he collects a claim. I agree with my colleague that if universality is a desirable feature of social insurance it must be applied on a consistent basis. I agree with everything that has been said in favour of this amendment.
I should like to refer briefly to some of the evidence presented before the committee. For example, in the submission by Robb Engineering on behalf of the contractors, we find a statement to the effect that it is unfair and unjust to apply experience rating to employers in the construction industry on the basis of lay-off patterns resulting from factors beyond the employer's control. I think that is the important phrase in that submission. It has been pointed out that most employers really have little or no control over their employment patterns. I do not believe they should be penalized for the lack of action or unfavourable action the government takes which affects their employment pattern.
What I should like to refer to specifically are the conclusions reached by the standing committee on the particular question of merit rating. While the committee's

June 11, 1971

report agreed that there should be a system of merit rating, the report was by no means unanimous; it was approved on division. However, even though they endorsed the principle of merit rating, they could not agree on it unanimously. Also, the committee stipulated that if we had to have some type of merit rating, it should be different from the type of merit rating proposed in this bill. This is not the final report, I think, but I believe the wording in the final report was basically the same. The report reads:
Indeed, the rating of a firm would seem to he more reasonable if based on the industry average instead of a national average. But there is absolutely no reason why one should not extend the experience rating system: an experience rating of industries defined on the basis of the national average and an experience rating of firms defined on the basis of the industry average. Industries could very well have an industry rate. This would provide a much more flexible system and one which would allow the basis of comparison to be fairer.
I simply want to ask the minister the following question, even though I do not approve of the principle of merit rating. I think I mentioned it in the committee and it seemed to me there was some disposition on the part of the minister or of the officials to study the whole question of merit rating. Possibly, by way of regulations, they might be able to break it down so that it would not work a hardship on all industries. As I said, I do not approve of the principle of merit rating, but half a loaf is better than none, and I would like to have an assurance from the minister that something will be done in this regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say only a few words in support of this motion, which I find very acceptable. That clause of the bill as well as the proposal of the white paper on which it is based have greatly surprised me and have caused some concern to a number of small employers in my area. In fact, if some employers have to lay-off one or many of their employees at certain times in the year, the cost of their contributions to the unemployment insurance fund will be higher. This is unfair to some small employers who, for one reason or another, do not enjoy the benefit of annual contracts.
There are, in my riding, road contractors, for instance, or forest contractors, who use heavy machinery and, at times, following a contract, need additional labour. When the contracts are completed and if they have no other work to carry out, they are obliged to let their employees go, sometimes temporarily, sometimes for a longer period. Under clause 65 of the legislation they will be penalized, that is, they will have to pay higher contributions to the unemployment insurance fund.
This is unfair to those employers, as well as to other employers, such as those in the construction business-as it was mentioned previously-who, at times, need additional labour. Then, should this clause be passed, those concerned might use other means in order to respect their contracts, and a number of workers will not find jobs, not even temporary ones, in those operations. Therefore, it is unfair to the workers, to the unemployed who want to work and who are looking for jobs.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
For all those reasons, although this matter has been considered at length in committee, even if we did not succeed in having this clause removed from the bill, if the minister wants to show the wisdom we know he has, it is important for him to consider all aspects of this clause. He will see then, I am sure, that there is more bad than good in it. I am therefore in favour of this motion which tends simply to remove clause 65 from this bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker. my remarks on this particular section will be brief. I listened with attention to hon. members. I think the contributions were all useful. Some have shown a very deep knowledge of the concept, but others, I am afraid, are not quite aware of what the bill intends. I do not say this sarcastically, but there is no real relationship between the original concept of merit rating that we envisaged in the white paper and the merit rating that is now in the bill. The merit rating system that is in the bill is really a compromise arrived at as a result of the contributions of members opposite on second reading and at the committee stage. The difficulty of the situation was perhaps amplified by the remarks made today by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-the unofficial minister of the socialist party. If he needs to be convinced about the merits of merit rating, he should read the very knowledgeable speech made on second reading by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman), indicating that even that party has mixed views and that they are not all quite as doctrinaire as might appear.

Merit rating does not, of course, have any relationship at all to the concept of universality. We all know this. We are not violating the concept of universality by introducing merit rating. Universaility simply means that all employees of companies so identified will be included in the plan, and it means that the widest spectrum of employees in the country will be included in the plan. What we are saying is that the employers in the country will have different rates based on the lay-off patterns in their particular industry. We are saying also that certain employees, despite the fact that this plan is universal, will be paying higher or lower contributions than others depending on what their normal income is at their place of employment.

June 11, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
That is what makes the concept of merit rating as we now have it acceptable to all members of the House, and I am surprised that there have been any amendments at all. Perhaps the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was persuaded by the CLC, but I must say in all fairness to the CLC that their view is based on fear, not logic. They feel-and perhaps I have greater confidence in employers than they do-that employers in some Machiavellian way may tend to keep the work staff as low as possible. I do not know too many employers who do not keep their work staff at the minimum possible level, I do not know too many employers who play Santa Claus and have a bigger staff than they need.

This is especially true if they wish to remain in business long. We talk about the Canadian Manufacturers Association opposing merit rating, but no one has yet mentioned that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce endorsed merit rating, indicating that there is a difference of opinion even among employers. But what makes the plan acceptable to everybody, possibly in line with what the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) pointed out, is that in order to assess the lay-off pattern of an industry we have eliminated all students hired. In other words, whether students are hired for one, two, five or ten weeks and then laid off, this will not affect the merit rating status of a company. Neither will its lay-off pattern be affected by maternity and sickness lay-off, voluntary withdrawals from its work force and those who are dismissed for misconduct.
To make it further acceptable to industry there has been a wide departure, I might say a dramatic departure, from what I first envisioned. I originally thought that through the marvels of the computer age it would be possible to merit-rate each individual company in the country, something which is quite feasible with the records and the computer systems which we have. What we are now proposing to do, and I think this meets the logical arguments that were advanced by hon. members opposite about the construction industry, is not to merit-rate the construction industry against industry in general but, rather, to compare companies in the industry with, or rate them against, the industry itself in general. What we are proposing to do is rate one company within the industry against the companies in general in that industry. In other words, if you had a private firm in the construction industry it would be rated against other private firms in that industry.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask one question in this regard. Canada being what it is, with its enormity of size and varying climatic conditions, would regional factors be taken into account in rating these businesses?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the type of observation I might answer as we go along. I am not unaware
of the problems of the construction industry. As Minister of Labour, I deal daily with components of that industry. I know their dependence on government; I know that many of them live on government contracts; I know that they are subject to the Labour (Standards) Code. They come to us time after time for exemptions against minimum wages, against the 40-hour work week and against the eight-hour day. These exemptions are given because of the nature of the industry. I think I understand their problems pragmatically, but there are always two sides to the coin when we talk about regions. When we had the winter works program in effect, contractors in British Columbia had a bonanza during the winter months as opposed to contractors in Quebec and Ontario who had to contend with severe climatic conditions.
In any event, we are not taking into consideration student employment, maternity or sickness leave, voluntary withdrawals or dismissals for misconduct in our merit rating; and in view of the fact that we are not going to rate companies in one industry against another industry we have made the proposal even more palatable. Further, this program will not come into effect until 1974, and even then only one-third of the effect will be felt, with the second thud to come along in 1975 and the last third in 1976.
In the interval between now and January, 1974, we have arranged for the utmost in co-operation and negotiation with the representatives of industry, through the advisory council. I think I have mentioned previously. Through regulations we can take into consideration the suggestion of the hon. member with respect to the problem of regional factors. These can be taken care of through regulations if the advisory council, the Unemployment Insurance Commission and representatives of the employers think that this is desirable.
Mr. Speaker, the merit rating that people may have feared for many reasons when it was first envisaged has very little resemblance to what we are now proposing. We are now proposing merit rating within an industry rather then with industry in general. We have eliminated the categories I have mentioned which could unduly distort the lay-off pattern of an industry. I do not look on this as a penalty against certain industries but, rather, as a reward to others; and I think this is the way the Chamber of Commerce looked at it.
Where the contribution now is 1.40 per 100, the figure in comparison will be 1.26. In fact, the cost to the employer and the employee is substantially lower under the new plan. Employers who have a fairly stable work pattern, such as school boards, municipalities, and secondary industry in general, will pay substantially less per individual than they are now paying. Some industries will pay a little higher than others, but their lay-off patterns will have to affect two-thirds of their employees in a year to really affect the cost of their unemployment insurance. When it is said that the lay-off of one or two employees would vary the rate, this indicates an ignorance of the bill: it would take as much as a two-thirds variation in work pattern to affect drastically the contributions required to be made.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take advantage of the indulgence of the House. I know that we want to finish this bill by four o'clock so I will just repeat that I recommend that we reject the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these are not significant amendments but they try to make the bill more presentable and get away from the arbitrary decisions that may have to be made by ministers involved-in this case I believe it is the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang). Clause 140 (2) (a) provides:
The minister shall collect Information concerning employment for workers and workers seeking employment and, to the extent the minister considers necessary,-
This is the part that we find offensive and arbitrary. It is left to the decision of the minister. In the amendment, the power of the minister to make a subjective evaluation as to when he will release information is deleted and the reasonably judicial test is substituted. If the government cannot go along with what I am suggesting, I hope they can give me reasons. I do not think I have to pursue this matter any further except to reiterate that the provision, "to the extent the minister considers necessary" should instead read, "to the extent reasonably necessary," which takes it away from the minister alone.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: If I could speak in support of this motion, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) is too modest when he refers to the proposed amendment as being somewhat insignificant. In many instances this Parliament delegates far too much authority to individual ministers of the Crown or to the executive branch in general. I think it has to be taken as a practical situation that the minister will probably never be the one to make the decision; it will be made by an administrator on his behalf.

The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) says that is just hearsay, but maybe he will be prepared to prove that statement by evidence. He probably will not attempt to do it at this time and it is unlikely that a convenient time will ever arise.
I am sure we have confidence in the present minister, but the fact is that ministers are not permanent and this legislation in all likelihood will stay on the statute books for many years. I suppose the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce intervened because this question deals with the collection of information. He is closely connected with the current census which is causing so much dissatisfaction among certain segments of the population, so he is probably somewhat sensitive on the subject.
In my view, the question of privacy arises here. All governments have a penchant for collecting information. They do this with the best intentions in the world, but in
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
many cases never use it and it just turns into a "make work" project. I suggest that any legislation along these lines should be based on the criteria of what is reasonably necessary. A great number of businessmen, small farmers and small businessmen in this country feel they are being driven to the wall by having to make voluminous returns to the government. Sometimes an examination of the questionnaire does not indicate what they are looking for. So I think a determined stand should be taken at every opportunity against this type of legislation which makes it easy for large staffs to be built up in departments for the collection of information even when there is no requirement or need for that information.
It is just not good enough to say, "where the minister considers it necessary". I think there will be further empire building if this legislation is passed. Empires are still being built. It is too bad that the government cannot institute more austerity programs. On the other hand, of course, our last austerity program did not have a great effect on empires built around the city and in federal government offices across the country.
Certainly, there has been no let-up in increasing the size of our bureaucracy. Bigger bureaucracy has led to increasing demands on bill payers in this country, the people who are trying to make a living, trying to make businesses grow and create jobs for other people. There has been a growing tide of demand on these people to meet administrative expenses which are really not justified nor necessary. I strongly urge the acceptance of this fine and important amendment moved by the hon. member for Hamilton West.

Mr. Speaker, if a vote is called on these two motions I shall probably vote for them, but I trust my friends will forgive me if I say I cannot get excited about the issue either way. May I abbreviate what is in the bill. It says that the minister shall collect certain information and, to the extent the minister considers necessary, he may make it available. The amendment would have the bill read- again I abbreviate-that the minister shall collect certain information and, to the extent reasonably necessary, make it available. Is there really any difference?
Perhaps my hon. friend will take me behind the curtain and point out to me just who is to decide, in the second case, what is "reasonably necessary". Surely, in the end it will be the minister who decides. I think the wording, as my hon. friend has suggested it, is less offensive. As I say, if there is a vote I shall probably support the amendment, but I do not think it is all that important.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak for a few minutes in defence of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). Perhaps because I live in a relatively small community with a Manpower office I can see events happening that hon. members who live in larger, more impersonal areas may not see. About 9,000 people live in
June 11, 1971

my town and employers who go to Manpower offices know a great deal, personally, about persons who are available for work. The same holds true of employees. The people of my community have access to a great deal of personal information.
Obviously, the minister cannot look after all the Manpower centres across the country. This means that his officials, including many small officials in lesser positions, will have to make these decisions. I therefore think it is most important for the word "reasonably" to be inserted in the clause. It would provide a defence against prosecution if certain officials consider that information which ought to be made available to them has not been made available.
I think the amendment is important from the point of view of personal privacy. This applies particularly to areas which are relatively small where the people know a great deal about each other. For this reason it is most important that the amendment be incorporated in the bill. The amendment would blunt administrative and bureaucratic trust and prevent officials from being overzealous. I think it is a useful amendment and hope the minister will accept it.
